## Archiving and registering a reanalysis {#every-reanalysis-leaves-a-public-trail .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
**OSF**, the Open Science Framework: a public repository in which data, code and **registrations** are timestamped and citable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
A registration is a **frozen, dated snapshot of a plan**. Anyone can check what you said you would do, and when.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
You need no account today. We are going to *read* OSF the way that reviewers do.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Multi100 itself was registered there: its scoring rules – same conclusion? effect size within ±0.05 *d*? – were filed **after the analysts had been recruited and before any analysis began**; 74% of the reanalyses reached the same conclusion, and 34% came within ±0.05 *d*.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
Preregistrations osf.io/4ev9t (pp. 2 and 9) and osf.io/y4evp; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness [p. 136].
:::

::: notes
Outside a classroom, an analysis plan is preregistered by filing it in a public registry. Everything you have worked with in this course – the dataset, my analysis script, the codebook – is kept at a permanent public address on the Open Science Framework. OSF does two jobs. It archives materials, which is the only reason you were able to stand in a real analyst's shoes at all. And it registers plans: a registration is a frozen, timestamped snapshot of what you intend to do, filed before you do it, that nobody – including you – can quietly edit afterwards. You do not need an account for any of this today. We are going to read OSF the way a reviewer or a sceptical reader would, starting with the public record of this paper. Multi100, the study in which you have been working as analyst no. 6, was itself registered there: the rules for judging the results, what counts as the same conclusion and how close is close for an effect size, were filed after the analysts had been recruited and before any of them had started, among them the rule that two results count as the same when their effect sizes lie within five hundredths of a Cohen's d. That is why the seventy-four per cent that reached the same conclusion and the thirty-four per cent that came within that band mean something, since nobody could move the goalposts once the results were in.
:::

## Three OSF addresses {#three-addresses-three-jobs}

::: {.urlbox}
[osf.io/8rtwe](https://osf.io/8rtwe) [– the archival Multi100 record: analyst C6HJR, frozen as submitted]{.fs-80}
:::

::: {.urlbox .fragment}
[osf.io/6zqct](https://osf.io/6zqct) [– the maintained fork: the script, the codebook, the course data]{.fs-80}
:::

::: {.urlbox .fragment}
[osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432) [– the full SCORE dossier on the EU-frames case: all the reports and their verdicts]{.fs-80}
:::

::: notes
Each of these does a different job. The first is the official archive: the Multi100 component for analyst C6HJR, frozen at the moment of submission and never touched again. That is what an archive is for, and it is also its limit, because an archive cannot be updated as a project moves on. The second address is the maintained fork, which is where the working materials are updated and where this course fetches its data from. A project that expects to keep changing usually needs both, an archive to preserve the record and a fork to keep the materials current. The third address is the full SCORE dossier on this paper, every reproduction report, the robustness study and the replication, all public, and the companion module on repositories reads it as a record.
:::

## Preregistration templates {#two-templates-one-choice}

::: {.small}
- In your report: the **AsPredicted short form**, adapted for data you already hold – eight plain-language questions (on OSF: "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org")
- The fuller tool for our job: the **secondary-data template** (van den Akker et al. 2021, *Meta-Psychology*) – 25 questions, built for reanalysing data you already hold
- Both templates are in your reading
:::

::: notes
There are two templates, and the course uses one of them. The block in your report follows the AsPredicted short form, eight questions in plain language written for people who have not collected data yet, so its first question has for us the awkward answer that I already hold everything. The secondary-data template of van den Akker and colleagues, twenty-five questions, was built for that situation, and our block borrows its section on what you already know about the data and calls it the data-in-hand statement.
:::

## The eight AsPredicted questions {#eight-questions-your-answers-already-mapped .smaller}

| AsPredicted asks | Your block answers |
|---|---|
| Q1 Have data been collected? | "It's complicated – I already hold them" + what I already know |
| Q2 Main question / hypothesis? | the claim, in your one sentence |
| Q3 Dependent variable? | your **frame set** and **scoring rule** |
| Q4 Conditions? | your options on the other decisions of the menu |
| Q5 Analyses? | your model + your support/undermine rule |
| Q6 Outliers / exclusions? | your **sample** decision |
| Q7 Sample size? | N = 270 country-years, fewer if your sample or series leaves some out |
| Q8 Anything else? | your DAG-grounded justification |

::: notes
Each AsPredicted question maps onto a decision from an earlier task, which is why the block takes about eight minutes rather than forty. The claim sentence you typed in chat earlier is question two. Your frame set and scoring rule make the dependent variable, question three. Your options on the other decisions of the menu are your conditions. Your sample decision is the exclusion rule. The sample size is two hundred and seventy country-years, fewer if your sample or your published series leaves some out. And the one question that AsPredicted handles badly for us, question one, you answer directly: the data exist, I hold them, and here is what I already know – including that the reproduced specification comes out at minus three point eight zero four.
:::
